title: Senior's toolkit: editing in verbs and nouns
summary: Change-inside, the dot command, block insert, confirmed substitutions and :g: the edits that make vim fast on real files.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: editing in verbs and nouns
steps.body: A verb plus a text object says exactly what to change, and `.` repeats it. These are the combinations experienced vim users type dozens of times a day.

toolkit.what: Change inside a word, quotes, brackets or an HTML/XML tag, wherever the cursor is in it. Replacing a value in a config line becomes three keys.
flags: around: includes the quotes, brackets or surrounding space
word, quotes, parens, braces, brackets, tag
toolkit.example: ci"  then type the new value, Esc

toolkit.what: Delete, copy or indent a whole paragraph (a block separated by blank lines), such as a function or a YAML block.
flags: a paragraph plus the blank line after it

toolkit.what: Repeats the last change. Make one good edit, then move (`n`, `j`, `;`) and press `.` where the same edit is needed.
flags: next match, same change: a manual find-and-replace with full control
toolkit.when: the same edit in several places that a regex would get wrong

toolkit.what: Undo and redo. vim keeps every change since the file was opened, so you can undo a long way back.
flags: the file as it was five minutes ago

toolkit.what: Block insert: select a column over several lines, insert text once, and it appears on every line. Comments out a block or adds a prefix.
flags: insert before / append after the block
append at the end of every line, even ragged ones
toolkit.example: Ctrl+V 5j I# Esc   (comments out six lines)

toolkit.what: Substitute across the whole file, asking at each match. The `c` keeps you safe on real files.
flags: every match on a line, not just the first
confirm each: y / n / a (all) / q

toolkit.what: Run a command on every line that matches (`:g`) or does not match (`:v`). Strips debug lines, or keeps only the errors in a pasted log.
flags: delete lines that do not match
run normal-mode keys on each match

toolkit.what: Copy to and paste from the system clipboard, when vim is built with clipboard support (`vim --version` shows `+clipboard`).
flags: paste the last yank, even after a delete

steps.prompt: Match each command to its effect.
pairs: replace the text between the quotes
delete the parentheses and what is inside
keep only the lines that contain ERROR
paste the last yank, not the last delete

steps.prompt: Rename `userId` to `customerId` everywhere in the file, as a whole word, confirming each one.
steps.explain: `%` is the whole file, `g` replaces every match on a line and `c` asks each time. The `\<` and `\>` stop it from also changing `userIdList`.

steps.prompt: Someone pasted 3,000 lines of log into a buffer and you only care about the lines containing `Timeout`. What do you type?
options: `/Timeout` and press `dd` on every other line
steps.explain: `:v` ("inverse global") deletes every line that does not match. `:g/Timeout/d` would do the opposite and throw your evidence away.

items: Rename a variable everywhere, checking each place
Put `# ` in front of eight lines of YAML
Redo one `ci(` edit inside a few different calls you jump to
Swap every `http://` for `https://` in a config
Add a column of `-` list markers
Wrap the same call in `await` at a few spots you visit by hand

steps.prompt: Comment out lines 10 to 14 of a shell script with a block insert, starting with the cursor on line 10, column 1.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Think in verb plus object (`ci"`, `dap`) and let `.` do the repeating. On anything you cannot easily undo, such as a shared config or a large file, add `c` to every substitution and check each match.
